RELEVANT CHARACTER BACKGROUND

José Almeida is in his late forties, with a graying beard and calloused hands from ten years tightening refrigerator compressors on a factory assembly line. He retired with a small pension and developed a deep aversion to routine. The factory taught him to see how repetition dulls dissent, how supervisors enforce obedience, and how the loudest voice often has the most to hide. He grew up in a working-class neighborhood in São Paulo’s Zona Leste; his father was a bricklayer, his mother a seamstress. They were devout Catholics but stopped attending mass after a priest embezzled parish funds, a memory that sharpens his skepticism. He values independence above all else—he refuses to join the artists’ union, calling it a “guild of gatekeepers”—yet he also craves connection: he knows the names of regular listeners and saves a seat for an elderly woman who brings him coffee. This tension defines him: he distrusts institutions but yearns for a community that shares his rage. For six months, he has performed daily monologues on Praça da Sé, arriving each morning at nine, unfolding a wooden crate, and speaking without introduction or microphone. He mimics voices, mocks corruption, and delivers cutting retorts to hecklers. He sleeps in a rented room nearby with a single bulb, a cot, and stacks of annotated newspapers. He has no phone or social media. When invited to organized groups, he has always declined after attending a single meeting, finding their rules or hierarchies suffocating. He routinely accepts small gestures of companionship—like the elderly woman’s coffee—without committing to ongoing arrangements. He has occasionally recited spontaneous verses at street festivals, but only when a crowd urged him and no formal stage existed.

OBJECTIVE SITUATION

After his morning monologue, a regular listener—a retired musician whom José calls Seu Olavo—invites him to join a roda de samba that meets every Sunday in a nearby square. Olavo says they need someone to recite verses between songs, and that the group is informal, with no dues or rules. José has never joined any group, but he misses the rhythm of factory whistles and the old sambas his mother hummed. He looks at his satchel, then at the afternoon stretching ahead.

PRE-APPRAISAL STATE AND ACCESSIBLE MEMORIES

José’s voice is slightly hoarse from the morning’s performance, and his left knee aches from standing on the cobblestones. He is carrying a slip of paper scrawled with notes for tomorrow’s monologue, which he had planned to write out this afternoon. A mild hunger gnaws at him, as he skipped breakfast to reread an editorial on rising utility prices. The phrase “roda de samba” triggers a memory of his mother humming “Morena dos Olhos d’Água” while sewing late into the night. Seu Olavo’s weathered hands remind José of the factory foreman who used to tap out rhythms on the assembly line during breaks.
